title: How Generative and Agentic AI Shift Concern from Technical Debt to Cognitive Debt
summary: Introduces cognitive debt, lost shared understanding that lives in developers' minds, as a bigger threat than technical debt under AI, and proposes slowing down and team practices to mitigate it.

assertions.quote: Cognitive debt is likely a much bigger threat than technical debt, as AI and agents are adopted.

verdicts.note: Naur's theory-building view and early studies of AI-assisted teams support loss of understanding as a real risk, but there is no measurement yet showing it outweighs technical debt.

assertions.quote: require that at least one human on the team fully understands each AI-generated change before it ships

verdicts.note: Ownership and maintainability require understanding; it's a reasonable review standard rather than an empirical finding.

assertions.quote: developers need to slow down and use practices such as pair programming, refactoring, and test-driven development to address technical debt AND cognitive debt.

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing engineering practices; strong fundamentals predict AI benefit.

assertions.quote: agents can also be used to manage cognitive load by summarizing what changes have been made and how

verdicts.note: Agents do speed onboarding and PR summarization, but surveys and the Anthropic learning study show many users skip understanding; outcome depends on use.

assertions.quote: Adding more agents to a project may add more coordination overhead, invisible decisions, and thus cognitive load.

verdicts.note: Many practitioner reports and some surveys describe higher intensity and fatigue from supervising agents, but controlled evidence is thin and other studies report reduced effort on routine work.
